source_text: MULTA et magna sunt, fratres charissimi beneficia divina quibus in salutem nostram Dei Patris et Christi larga et copiosa clementia et operata sit et semper operetur, quod conservandis ac vivificandis nobis Pater Filium misit, ut reparare nos posset, quodque Filius missus esse et hominis filius fieri voluit ut nos Dei filios faceret. Humiliavit se, ut populum qui prius jacebat erigeret: vulneratus est, ut vulnera nostra curaret: servivit, ut ad libertatem servientes extraheret: mori sustinuit, ut immortalitatem mortalibus exhiberet. Multa haec sunt et magna divinae misericordiae munera. Sed adhuc, qualis providentia illa et quanta clementia est quod nobis salutari ratione prospicitur, ut homini qui redemptus est reservando plenius consulatur! Nam, cum Dominus adveniens sanasset illa quae Adam portaverat vulnera, et venena serpentis antiqua curasset, legem dedit sano, et praecepit ne ultra jam peccaret, ne quid peccanti gravius eveniret. Coarctati eramus et in angustum innocentiae praescriptione conclusi. Nec haberet quid fragilitatis humanae infirmitas atque imbecillitas faceret, nisi iterum pietas divina subveniens, justitiae et misericordiae operibus ostensis, viam quamdam tuendae salutis aperiret, ut sordes postmodum, quascumque contrahimus, eleemosynis abluamus. Loquitur in Scripturis divinis Spiritus sanctus et dicit: Eleemosynis et fide delicta purgantur. Non utique illa delicta quae fuerant ante contracta, nam illa Christi sanguine et sanctificatione purgantur. Item denuo dicit: Sicut aqua extinguit ignem, sic eleemosyna extinguit peccatum. Hic quoque ostenditur et probatur quia, sicut lavacro aquae salutaris gehennae ignis extinguitur, ita et eleemosynis atque operationibus justis delictorum flamma sopitur. Et quia semel in Baptismo remissa peccatorum datur, assidua et jugis operatio Baptismi instar imitata, Dei rursus indulgentiam largitur. Hoc et in Evangelio Dominus docet. Nam cum denotarentur discipuli ejus quod ederent, nec prius manus abluissent, respondit et dixit: Qui fecit quod intus est, fecit et quod foris est. Verum date eleemosynam, et ecce vobis munda omnia: docens scilicet et ostendens non manus lavandas esse, sed pectus, et sordes intrinsecus potius quam extrinsecus detrahendas; verum qui purgaverit quod est intus, eum quoque id quod foris est repurgasse, et emundata mente, cute quoque et corpore mundum esse coepisse. Porro autem, monens et ostendens unde mundi et purgati esse possimus, addidit eleemosynas esse faciendas. Misericors docet et monet misericordiam fieri; et quia servare quaerit quos magno pretio redemit, post Baptismi gratiam sordidatos docet denuo posse purgari. Agnoscamus itaque, fratres charissimi, divinae indulgentiae munus salubre, et emundandis purgandisque peccatis nostris, qui sine aliquo conscientiae vulnere esse non possumus, medelis spiritalibus vulnera nostra curemus. Nec quisquam sic sibi de puro atque immaculato pectore blandiatur, ut, innocentia sua fretus, medicinam non putet adhibendam esse vulneribus, cum scriptum sit: Quis gloriabitur castum se habere cor, aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a peccatis? et iterum in Epistola sua Joannes ponat et dicat: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est. Si autem nemo esse sine peccato potest, et quisquis inculpatum se esse dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est, quam necessaria, quam benigna est divina clementia, quae, cum sciat non deesse sanatis quaedam postmodum vulnera, dedit curandis denuo sanandisque vulneribus remedia salutaria! Numquam denique, fratres dilectissimi, admonitio divina cessavit et tacuit quominus in Scripturis sanctis tam veteribus quam novis semper et ubique ad misericordiae opera Dei populus provocaretur; et canente atque exhortante Spiritu sancto, quisquis ad spem regni coelestis instruitur, facere eleemosynas jubetur. Mandat et praecipit Esaiae Deus: Exclama, inquit, in fortitudine, et noli parcere. Sicut tuba exalta vocem tuam, et annuntia plebi meae peccata ipsorum et domui Jacob facinora eorum. Et cum peccata eis sua exprobrari praecepisset, cumque eorum facinora pleno indignationis impetu protulisset, dixissetque eos nec, si orationibus et precibus et jejuniis uterentur, satisfacere pro delictis posse, nec, si in cilicio et cinere volverentur, iram Dei posse lenire, in novissima tamen parte, demonstrans solis eleemosynis Deum posse placari, addidit dicens: Frange esurienti panem tuum, et egenos sine tecto induc in domum tuam. Si videris nudum, vesti eum, et domesticos seminis tui non despicias. Tunc erumpet temporaneum lumen tuum, et vestimenta tua cito orientur, et praeibit ante te justitia, et claritas Dei circumdabit te. Tunc exclamabis, et Deus exaudiet te. Dum adhuc loqueris dicet: Ecce adsum.
pass_a_gloss: Many and great are the divine benefits by which the abundant and rich clemency of God the Father and Christ has been and is always at work for our salvation, because the Father sent the Son to preserve and give life to us, so that He might restore us, and because the Son willed to be sent and to become the son of man, so that He might make us sons of God. He humbled Himself, so that He might raise up the people who were previously lying down; He was wounded, so that He might heal our wounds; He served, so that He might lead those serving into freedom; He endured death, so that He might show immortality to mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy. But, moreover, what kind of providence and how great is the clemency that is provided for us with a saving plan, so that the person who has been redeemed might be more fully consulted? For when the Lord, coming, had healed the wounds that Adam had borne, and had cured the ancient poisons of the serpent, He gave a law to the healthy, and commanded that they should not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to the sinner. We were restricted and enclosed in a narrow prescription of innocence. And human fragility and weakness would have nothing to do, unless divine piety, assisting again, might show works of justice and mercy, and open a certain way of safeguarding salvation, so that we might wash away the filth that we contract afterwards with alms. The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: Sins are purified by alms and faith. Not, indeed, those sins that were contracted before, for those are purified by the blood and sanctification of Christ. Again, He says: Just as water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguish sin. Here, also, it is shown and proven that, just as the fire of Gehenna is extinguished by the bath of saving water, so also the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. And because once in Baptism the remission of sins is given, a constant and daily operation, imitating Baptism, again obtains God's indulgence. The Lord teaches this also in the Gospel. For when His disciples were rebuked because they were eating without washing their hands, He responded and said: He who made what is inside, also made what is outside. But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you; teaching, namely, and showing that it is not the hands that need to be washed, but the breast, and that the filth inside rather than outside needs to be removed; and that he who purifies what is inside, also purifies what is outside, and with a cleansed mind, he has also begun to be clean in body and skin. Furthermore, warning and showing from where we can be clean and purified, He added that alms need to be given. The Merciful One teaches and warns to practice mercy; and because He seeks to save those whom He redeemed at a great price, after the grace of Baptism, He teaches that those who have been stained can again be purified. Let us therefore recognize, dear brothers, the healthy gift of divine indulgence, and let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies, so that we may be cleansed and purified from our sins, since we cannot be without any wound of conscience. And let no one flatter himself about having a pure and immaculate breast, so that, trusting in his own innocence, he might not think that medicine needs to be applied to wounds, since it is written: Who boasts of having a chaste heart, or who boasts of being free from sins? And again, John says in his Epistle: If we say that we do not have sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if no one can be without sin, and whoever says that he is blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary and kind is divine clemency, which, knowing that the healthy do not lack some wounds afterwards, has given remedies for healing and saving wounds again! Finally, dear brothers, the divine admonition has never ceased and been silent, so that in the holy Scriptures, both old and new, the people of God might always and everywhere be provoked to the works of mercy; and with the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms. God commands and orders Isaiah: Cry out, He says, with strength, and do not spare. Lift up your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their wicked deeds. And when He had commanded that their sins be rebuked, and their wicked deeds be brought forth with a full impulse of indignation, and had said that they could not satisfy for their sins even with prayers and supplications and fasts, nor could they placate the wrath of God even by rolling in sackcloth and ashes, yet in the last part, showing that God can be placated only by alms, He added, saying: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise the members of your family. Then your light will break forth, and your garments will quickly arise, and justice will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking, He will say: Behold, I am present.

pass_b_english: Countless and tremendous are the divine benefits through which the rich and abundant clemency of God the Father and Christ has worked and continues to work for our salvation. The Father sent the Son to preserve and give us life so that He might restore us, and the Son willed to be sent and to become the Son of Man so that He might make us sons of God. He humbled Himself to raise up the people who lay prostrate; He was wounded to heal our wounds; He became a servant to lead servants into freedom; He endured death to offer immortality to mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy. But consider further: what kind of providence, how great a clemency, plans for us with a saving purpose so that the redeemed person might be more fully provided for? When the Lord came, He healed the wounds Adam bore and cured the ancient venom of the serpent. He gave a law to the healed and commanded them not to sin again, lest something worse befall the sinner. We were confined, shut in by a narrow prescription of innocence. Human frailty and weakness would have had no recourse unless divine pity came to our aid once more, displaying works of justice and mercy and opening a way to safeguard salvation, so that we might wash away whatever filth we contract afterwards through alms. The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: "Sins are purified by alms and faith" — not the sins contracted before, for those are purified by the blood and sanctification of Christ. He says again: "Just as water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguishes sin." Here it is shown and proven that, just as the fire of Gehenna is quenched by the bath of saving water, so the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. Because the remission of sins is given once in Baptism, a constant and daily practice that imitates Baptism again obtains God's indulgence. The Lord teaches this also in the Gospel. When His disciples were rebuked for eating without washing their hands, He answered: "The One who made the inside also made the outside. But give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you" (Luke 11:41). He was teaching and showing that it is not the hands that need washing, but the heart, and that the filth inside rather than outside must be removed; the one who purifies the inside also purifies the outside, and with a cleansed mind he begins to be clean in skin and body as well. Furthermore, warning us and showing from what source we can be clean and purified, He added that alms must be given. The Merciful One teaches and urges us to practice mercy; because He seeks to save those He redeemed at a great price, He teaches that those stained after the grace of Baptism can be purified again. Let us therefore recognize, dear brothers, the wholesome gift of divine indulgence, and let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies so that we may be cleansed and purified from our sins, since we cannot exist without some wound of conscience. No one should flatter himself about having a pure and spotless heart, trusting his own innocence to think medicine need not be applied to wounds, since it is written: "Who can boast of having a chaste heart, or who can boast of being free from sins?" And again John says in his Epistle: "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." If no one can be without sin, and whoever claims to be blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary and kind is divine clemency, which knows that the healed do not lack subsequent wounds and has given remedies to heal and save those wounds again! Finally, dear brothers, the divine admonition has never ceased or fallen silent, so that in the holy Scriptures, both old and new, the people of God might always and everywhere be urged to works of mercy; and with the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms. God commands and orders Isaiah: "Cry out with strength, do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their wicked deeds" (Isaiah 58:1). When He had commanded that their sins be rebuked and their wicked deeds laid bare with full indignation, and had said they could not satisfy for their sins even with prayers, supplications, and fasts, nor placate God's wrath even by wearing sackcloth and ashes, yet in the final passage He showed that God can be appeased only by alms, adding: "Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; if you see the naked, clothe him, and do not hide from your own flesh" (Isaiah 58:7). Then your light will break forth like the dawn, your healing will spring up quickly, your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will be your rear guard. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry for help, and He will say: Here I am (Isaiah 58:8-9).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the required scripture citations (Luke 11:41, Isaiah 58:1, Isaiah 58:7, Isaiah 58:8-9) which correspond to the quoted/alluded passages in the Latin. Pass A is a faithful literal rendering. The title 'Divine Mercy and Almsgiving' correctly names the thought of the treatise.
